clue.text: Ideal situation for the eavesdropper.

parts.note: a place set up for hearing others' talk, such as a forward military post for picking up enemy signals, is just where a snooper would want to be

explanation.surface: A tip on where best to stand if you want to overhear secrets.
explanation.definitionFit: An intelligence station set up to intercept messages is exactly a spot for overhearing others.

clue.text: Just a chap who looks in.

definitions.text: Just a chap who looks in

parts.words: Just a chap who looks in
parts.note: 'looks in' suggests a casual visitor dropping by, but it means a man whose gaze is turned inward on himself

explanation.surface: A modest description of a man who pops round for a visit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Looks in' reads as calling on someone; here it means looking inward, at one's own thoughts.
explanation.definitionFit: A shy, inward-looking personality is the psychologist's term for someone focused on their own mind.

clue.text: An odd description of one who has been on the loose!

definitions.text: An odd description of one who has been on the loose!

parts.words: An odd description of one who has been on the loose!
parts.note: someone out on a spree, letting loose, ends up drunk, and the slang word for drunk is the opposite of loose, hence 'odd'

explanation.surface: A remark on how strangely we label someone who has been out running wild.
explanation.walkthrough: The oddity is that a man who has been 'on the loose' gets described with a word meaning the reverse of loose, slang for drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for intoxicated, the state of a reveller after a night out.

clue.text: A strike? Only ten per cent, out.

definitions.text: A strike? Only ten per cent, out.

parts.words: A strike? Only ten per cent, out.
parts.note: a strike in bowling knocks every pin down; take ten per cent away from a set of ten pins and one is gone, leaving a game played with one pin fewer

explanation.surface: A question about industrial action where only a tenth of the workforce has walked out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strike' and 'out' suggest a labour dispute, but this is skittles: ten pins less ten per cent leaves the old skittles game played with one fewer than ten.
explanation.definitionFit: An old skittles game played with a set of pins one short of the modern bowling ten.

clue.text: Plaint of the unsuccessful punter.

parts.note: a punter is a gambler on horses, and the losing bettor's complaint is that fortune did not favour him

explanation.surface: The lament of a gambler whose horse has lost.
explanation.walkthrough: A punter, in British usage, is someone who bets on horses.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a stock complaint meaning fortune failed someone, just what a losing gambler mutters.

clue.text: Frank admissions as to time and place.

definitions.text: Frank admissions as to time and place

parts.words: Frank admissions as to time and place
parts.note: to frank a letter is to stamp it, and the franking stamp records when and where it was posted, so it is a 'frank admission' of time and place

explanation.surface: A suspect's honest confession of where they were and when.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank admissions' sounds like a candid confession; 'frank' is the postal verb for stamping a letter, which records date and office.
explanation.definitionFit: The ink stamps on envelopes show the date and the sorting office where mail was processed.

clue.text: A bad lapse; but it's just part of the 'whole bloomer.

indicators.note: a bad lapse is a poor one, and 'bad' here signals that the word lapse is rearranged

explanation.surface: A blunder that turns out to be only a fraction of a bigger mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomer' is British slang for a blunder, which fits 'lapse', but here it means a flower; 'bad' shuffles LAPSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Each leaf-like segment of a flower's outer calyx is one component of the whole blossom.

clue.text: The sort of matter that can lead to fall-out if not properly handled.

definitions.text: The sort of matter that can lead to fall-out if not properly handled

parts.words: The sort of matter that can lead to fall-out if not properly handled
parts.note: 'matter' and 'fall-out' suggest radioactive material, but the matter is a disputed topic and fall-out is a quarrel between people

explanation.surface: A warning about radioactive material that will spread contamination if mishandled.
explanation.walkthrough: The nuclear picture of matter and fall-out misleads: the clue means a subject that can make people fall out.
explanation.definitionFit: A disputed, divisive topic can cause people to quarrel if handled clumsily.

clue.text: The roll of the liner-from the traveller's angle, perhaps?

definitions.text: The roll of the liner-from the traveller's angle, perhaps?

parts.words: The roll of the liner-from the traveller's angle, perhaps?
parts.note: the ship's rolling seems to be a seasick traveller's view, but a roll is also a register of names, here those of everyone sailing on the liner

explanation.surface: How the pitching and rolling of an ocean liner feels to someone on board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roll' looks like a ship's motion; it is a list of names, the register of those aboard.
explanation.definitionFit: A shipping line keeps a register naming everyone booked aboard a voyage.

clue.text: Strangely enough, a long coat with sides of four-by-two.

indicators.note: something strange is out of its usual order, so the letters of a long coat are rearranged

explanation.surface: A peculiar observation about a long coat cut with an odd number of panels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Four-by-two' suggests a timber size, but it is a sum: four times two sides makes an eight-sided figure.
explanation.definitionFit: Four times two is eight, and an eight-sided shape is described by this word.

clue.text: Having selected this, one must only expect to get browned off.

definitions.text: Having selected this, one must only expect to get browned off.

parts.words: Having selected this, one must only expect to get browned off.
parts.note: 'browned off' means fed up, but here it is literal: choosing this photographic tint or ink makes the result come out brown

explanation.surface: A grumble that whoever made this choice deserves to end up fed up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Browned off' is British slang for fed up; the clue means turned brown, as with the reddish-brown tone of old photographs.
explanation.definitionFit: A reddish-brown pigment, once made from cuttlefish ink, used to tint photographs.

clue.text: Here comes the that must be caught with tickling." (Twelfth Night).

definitions.text: Here comes the that must be caught with tickling." (Twelfth Night).

parts.words: Here comes the that must be caught with tickling." (Twelfth Night).
parts.note: Maria's line in Shakespeare's Twelfth Night, as Malvolio approaches, compares him to a fish that poachers catch by stroking its belly

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare's comedy with a word left out for the solver to supply.
explanation.walkthrough: The missing word fills the gap in Maria's line in Twelfth Night; tickling is a poacher's way of catching a river fish by hand.
explanation.definitionFit: A freshwater game fish, traditionally caught by hand by stroking its underside.

clue.text: Cram in some loose slippers; they'll take the weight when the road is rough and steep.

definitions.text: they'll take the weight when the road is rough and steep

parts.note: to cram things in is to pack them
mules are backless slippers that sit loosely on the foot

explanation.surface: Advice to stuff some slippers into a bag before a hard mountain trek.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loose slippers' seems to want an anagram of slippers; it is a definition of backless slippers.
explanation.definitionFit: Hybrid beasts of burden carry loads along steep mountain tracks.

clue.text: By no means rare moment for change of bowling.

definitions.meaning: meat cooked far past rare is cooked too long
in cricket the bowling switches ends when a set of six balls is finished, so the moment is when that set is completed

explanation.surface: A remark on when a steak is ready, paired with a cricket captain's switch of bowler.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an over is six balls, and when it is done the next one is bowled from the other end, often by a different bowler.
explanation.definitionFit: Meat cooked too long is far from rare; and in cricket, when an over is finished, the bowling changes ends.

clue.text: This really sets off something French and in the one who makes the gift.

indicators.note: the French word is placed inside the giver

parts.words: the one who makes the gift
parts.note: a donator is a giver of a gift
et is the French word for and

explanation.surface: A tribute to a generous benefactor who launches some French venture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This really sets off something' reads as praise; it is the definition, a device that triggers an explosion.
explanation.definitionFit: A device used to trigger an explosive charge is what sets a blast going.

clue.text: State in which the raw material has almost vanished.

parts.note: ore is the raw rock from which metal is extracted

indicators.note: almost means the last letter of the word is cut off

parts.note: gone means vanished

explanation.surface: A US state where the natural resources have nearly run out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' cuts the final E from GONE, giving GON.
explanation.definitionFit: A Pacific Northwest member of the United States.

clue.text: One could emerge rug and all from this kind of fever.

indicators.note: letters that emerge in a new form are rearranged, so rug and all is reshuffled

explanation.surface: A picture of a patient recovering from fever, rising from the sickbed with the rug still round them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could emerge' rearranges the nine letters RUG AND ALL; glandular fever is the British name for mononucleosis.
explanation.definitionFit: Glandular fever is the British name for infectious mononucleosis.

clue.text: Regarded as a fast, aggressive fighter, sought ', fortune abroad.

parts.note: the MiG is a Soviet-designed jet fighter aircraft
to be regarded as something is to be rated as it

explanation.surface: A description of someone thought of as a fierce combatant who went overseas to make their name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fighter' suggests a boxer or soldier, but it is the Soviet jet. 'Regarded' comes first in the clue though its piece ends the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Moving to another country to seek one's fortune is to relocate abroad.

clue.text: A large holding to be concerned in so modest a test.

indicators.note: to be concerned in something is to be involved within it, so the answer is found inside the words

explanation.surface: A large property bound up in a humble examination.
explanation.definitionFit: A large landed property with its house and grounds is a big landholding.

clue.text: Warm and dry interval, but It's susceptible:..of international violation.

parts.note: to air linen is to warm and dry it
a space is an interval or gap

explanation.surface: A forecast of a warm dry spell between bouts of rain, oddly linked to a diplomatic incident.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Warm and dry interval' looks like a weather report; it is two pieces. Foreign aircraft entering a nation's skies without permission violate it.
explanation.definitionFit: The sky above a country's territory is sovereign, and unauthorised foreign aircraft can breach it.

clue.text: A somewhat defiant presentation of arms.

definitions.text: A somewhat defiant presentation of arms

parts.words: A somewhat defiant presentation of arms
parts.note: a soldier's 'present arms' is a salute with a rifle, but here the arms are human ones, held with hands on hips and elbows out

explanation.surface: A soldier showing reluctant disrespect during a rifle salute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Presentation of arms' suggests the military salute; it means holding one's arms in a stance, hands on hips and elbows outward.
explanation.definitionFit: Hands on hips with elbows turned out is a posture suggesting challenge or impatience.

clue.text: Just the thing for a good blow out at the races.

definitions.text: Just the thing for a good blow out at the races

parts.words: Just the thing for a good blow out at the races
parts.note: a 'blow-out' is a big meal or party, but here the blowing is wind filling a sail during yacht races

explanation.surface: A recommendation for a lavish feast at a race meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blow out' suggests a slap-up meal at the horse races; the races are yacht races and the blow is wind billowing a large sail out front.
explanation.definitionFit: A large balloon-shaped sail set at the bow of a racing yacht to catch a following wind.

clue.text: "What act, 'That roars so loud, 11 and thunders in the (Hamlet):

definitions.text: "What act, 'That roars so loud, 11 and thunders in the (Hamlet):

parts.words: "What act, 'That roars so loud, 11 and thunders in the (Hamlet):
parts.note: the Queen's question to Hamlet in the closet scene ends with a word meaning the preface or opening of a book, which the solver supplies

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare's tragedy with its final word left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: Gertrude asks 'Ay me, what act, That roars so loud and thunders in the index?' In Shakespeare's day the word meant a prologue or table of contents at the front of a book.
explanation.definitionFit: Here used in its old sense of a prologue or introductory list at the front of a book.

clue.text: Right lady to go back for water up north.

indicators.note: going back means the word lady is read from end to start

parts.note: taken as written before being turned

explanation.surface: Directions telling the correct woman to return north to the lakes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to go back' turns LADY into YDAL. Rydal Water is a small lake in England's Lake District, in the north-west.
explanation.definitionFit: Rydal Water is a small lake in Cumbria's Lake District, in northern England.

clue.text: Clearly not one for the outside job, this-bird.

definitions.text: Clearly not one for the outside job, this-bird.

parts.words: Clearly not one for the outside job, this-bird.
parts.note: an outside job is a burglary done by a stranger; split the bird's name and it says it steals from within, an inside job

explanation.surface: A remark that a particular small bird is unsuited to working outdoors.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as ROB IN, the bird's name describes theft from the inside, so it is plainly no outside job.
explanation.definitionFit: A small red-breasted songbird familiar in British gardens.

clue.text: Kind of ale to put to the test.

definitions.meaning: a strong ale formerly brewed at Oxford and Cambridge colleges for the day accounts were settled
to examine accounts formally is to check them

explanation.surface: A suggestion to try out a particular beer.
explanation.walkthrough: Audit ale was a strong beer brewed in Oxford and Cambridge colleges, served on the day tenants' accounts were examined.
explanation.definitionFit: A college ale named after the day accounts were checked; and an official examination of accounts tests them.

clue.text: Lethal grub provisions for insect dances?

definitions.meaning: small balls of camphor or naphthalene stored with clothes kill the larvae that eat cloth
a ball is a formal dance, so dances held by fluttering night insects

explanation.surface: Deadly food supplies laid on for a party of bugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grub' looks like food; it is a larva, and the 'provisions' are what is provided to kill it.
explanation.definitionFit: Naphthalene pellets kept with clothes kill cloth-eating larvae; read as two words, they are dances for night-flying insects.

clue.text: Somewhat unusual suffragan bishop, perhaps.

definitions.meaning: rather out of the ordinary, remarkable
a bishop is an 'ordinary' in church law, and a suffragan is an additional, assisting one

explanation.surface: A remark that an assistant bishop is a bit of an oddity.
explanation.walkthrough: In church law a diocesan bishop is an 'ordinary'; a suffragan, assisting him, is an extra one, so the answer splits as EXTRA ORDINARY.
explanation.definitionFit: Remarkable or out of the ordinary; and an assistant bishop is an additional church 'ordinary'.
